t.kathmandu@27.7,85.3:
It is a place that overwhelms at first, with narrow lanes, shrines on every corner, motorbikes and tuk-tuks, and the smell of incense, diesel and frying dough. On a clear morning, snow peaks appear to the north, a surprise after the haze.

The Prithvi Highway starts here and runs west to Pokhara, about two hundred kilometres, through some of the loveliest and most chaotic riding in Asia. It climbs out of the valley over the rim, drops into the gorge of the Trishuli river and follows it, with tight bends, steep slopes and trucks and buses that overtake on blind corners. The surface can be rough, with potholes, landslides in the monsoon and long delays at bad sections. A day's ride can take seven or eight hours or more, so start early, ride defensively and be ready for sudden stops. Nepali traffic drives on the left.

The valley has an extraordinary heritage. Durbar Square, with its carved wooden temples, was badly damaged in the 2015 earthquake, and restoration continues. Swayambhunath, a hilltop stupa with watching eyes, is known as the Monkey Temple, and Boudhanath, one of the largest stupas in the world, is the centre of Tibetan Buddhism in Nepal. Pashupatinath, a Hindu temple complex on the Bagmati river, is a place of cremations and pilgrimage. The city's Newar people have a rich cuisine, with momo dumplings and spiced meat dishes.

Fuel is available in Kathmandu, but shortages occur from time to time, so fill up whenever you can. There are stations along the highway, though the supply is not always reliable. Cafes and small restaurants serve dal bhat, the rice and lentil meal that is the national dish.

Carry a mask for the dust and keep your visor clean. A good start in the early morning, before the traffic, makes the day easier.
t.paro@27.4,89.4:
Paro lies on a broad, flat valley floor at roughly twenty-two hundred metres in western Bhutan, which makes it the most civilised-looking place in a country of narrow gorges and steep forests. The Paro Chhu river runs through a patchwork of rice fields, and farmhouses with painted windows and carved wooden eaves sit among apple orchards, with pine-covered mountains on either side. The country's only international airport is here, and the approach, threading between peaks with the pilot flying by sight, is considered one of the trickiest in the world.

Paro is also where Bhutan's spiritual landmarks cluster. High on a cliff about nine hundred metres above the valley floor, Paro Taktsang, the Tiger's Nest monastery, clings to a rock face as though glued, and the story is that Guru Rinpoche flew there on the back of a tigress in the eighth century to meditate in a cave. The hike takes a few hours each way and is steep. Down in the valley, Rinpung Dzong, a massive whitewashed fortress-monastery with a covered wooden bridge in front, was built in the seventeenth century and still houses monks and the district administration. In spring it hosts a famous festival with masked dances.

Visitors normally travel on an organised tour with a licensed guide, and foreign-plated vehicles and rider arrangements are tightly controlled, so check the current rules with an operator long before you plan anything. If you can arrange it, the East-West Highway, known as the Lateral Road, starts from here and runs over high passes with prayer flags, through cloud forest and past monasteries, on a road that is narrow, steep and subject to landslides in the monsoon, from June to September.

Paro has fuel and basic services, though the town has fewer than three thousand people, and Thimphu, the capital, about an hour's drive to the east, has more of everything.

Try the national dish, ema datshi, chillies in cheese sauce, with red rice, and be prepared for it to be hot. Arrive with acclimatised lungs, because the altitude shows when you climb stairs.
t.thimphu@27.5,89.6:
Thimphu is a capital city with no traffic lights. The government has decided that the lights would spoil the town's character, and at the main crossing a policeman in white gloves directs the cars with elegant, slow gestures. The city of about a hundred thousand lies in a valley at around 2,300 metres, along the Wang Chhu river, with prayer flags fluttering on the hillsides and the great white and gold dzong, the fortress that serves as the seat of government and the home of the monastic body, standing beside the river. Most buildings are built in the traditional style, with painted wooden windows and sloping roofs, as required by law.

The Buddha Dordenma, an enormous gilded statue on a hill above the city, looks over the valley and is a gathering place at dusk. Archery, the national sport, is practised at the Changlimithang ground, and the competitors in traditional dress shoot at targets over a hundred metres away, to the sound of singing and teasing from the opposing team. The weekend market by the river sells vegetables, red rice, dried cheese and chillies, which are a Bhutanese staple, and is a good place to see the country's variety.

Motorcycling in Bhutan is regulated. Foreign visitors travel with a licensed tour operator and a guide, pay a daily fee, and need permits for the route, so independent riding is not possible, and it is worth planning ahead. The roads are mountain roads with hairpin bends, steep drops and few guardrails, and landslides in the monsoon from June to September are common. The best seasons are spring and autumn, when the skies are clear and the rhododendrons or the autumn colours are in glory. Speed is low, partly because the road demands it and partly because there is no need to hurry.

Thimphu has fuel stations, workshops and plenty of cafes, and it is the last place with a full range of services before the long road east. Paro, with its airport, lies about twenty-three kilometres away. Take time for a bowl of ema datshi, chillies in cheese sauce, which is the national dish and is often hotter than expected, and drink butter tea to take the edge off the cold. Evenings are chilly, and in winter frost covers the ground in the morning.
t.dochula pass@27.5,89.8:
Dochula Pass lies at 3,100 metres on the road between Thimphu and Punakha, and it is the first big climb eastward out of the capital. The road leaves the valley and winds up through forest of blue pine and rhododendron, in a long series of hairpin bends, to a saddle hung with thousands of prayer flags. Mist often fills the pass in the morning, giving the place a hushed, otherworldly look, and the temperature drops sharply, so a warm layer is needed even in summer.

On the pass stand one hundred and eight chortens, small stupas arranged in a mound, built in the early 2000s in honour of Bhutanese soldiers who had died in a military operation, and on behalf of the country's peace. A temple stands close by, and the whole site is a place of quiet reverence, where visitors walk clockwise around the stupas and spin prayer wheels. A festival is held here each December, with masked dances. On a clear day, especially in autumn and winter, the view opens to the great Himalayan peaks to the north, a long line of snow summits above the green ridges.

The road is the thing for a rider. The climb from Thimphu is steady and well surfaced, with sharp bends and gradients that call for care, and the descent to Punakha on the east side drops more than two thousand metres to a warm, subtropical valley in less than three hours. The change in vegetation is striking, from cold conifers to rice terraces and banana trees. Mist, rain and landslides can interrupt the route, particularly in the monsoon from June to September, and it is vital to keep to a moderate speed, and to expect cattle and trucks on blind corners.

A small cafe and snack stand at the pass sells hot tea and noodles, and the views are the reason to stop. Early morning gives the best chance of clear skies, though it is also the coldest. Yaks graze on the high slopes in winter, and prayer flags flutter in constant wind, sending their blessings across the valley.
t.punakha@27.6,89.9:
Punakha sits at the meeting of two rivers, the Pho Chhu and the Mo Chhu, the father and mother rivers, and the great dzong of Punakha stands on the tongue of land between them, its whitewashed walls and gold roofs reflected in the water. It was built in the seventeenth century by Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal, the founder of the Bhutanese state, and served as the capital until the middle of the twentieth century. It remains the winter home of the monastic body. Reaching it involves crossing a long wooden cantilever bridge, with prayer flags overhead, and the approach is memorable.

The valley lies at around 1,200 metres, much lower and warmer than Thimphu, and the climate is subtropical. Terraced rice fields step down the hillsides in green or gold depending on the season, with banana, orange and chilli plants beside the houses. In spring the jacaranda trees around the dzong bloom a soft purple, a contrast to the white walls. A suspension bridge, hung with prayer flags and one of the longest in Bhutan, spans the Pho Chhu, and it is a pleasant walk to cross it, with a view of the river below.

Not far off, across the rice fields, stands the temple of Chimi Lhakhang, associated with the Divine Madman, Drukpa Kunley, a fifteenth-century saint known for his unorthodox methods, and where couples go to receive blessings for fertility. The village approaches are decorated with painted phalluses on the walls, a Bhutanese tradition of protection that startles first-time visitors.

For a rider, the road down from Dochula is a long descent with fine views, and the approach to Punakha is a relief after the cold of the pass. The road is paved and well maintained, though landslides can occur in the monsoon, and the temperature climbs as you descend, so you may want to remove a layer. Look out for cattle on the road and for trucks on the narrow bends. Punakha has a few fuel stations, small hotels, and restaurants serving red rice, chilli and cheese, and fresh river fish. The best seasons are March and April, when the flowers bloom, and October to November, when the skies are clear. Summer is hot and humid, with monsoon rain.
t.nathu la@27.4,88.8:
Nathu La is a mountain pass on the border between Sikkim and Tibet, at 4,310 metres, and it carries more history than its modest size suggests. It was part of an old trade route that linked Lhasa with the plains of Bengal, one of the tributaries of what people now loosely call the Silk Route, along which wool, salt, tea and silver moved by mule. The pass closed after the 1962 war between India and China and stayed shut for decades. It reopened for border trade in 2006, and today the two armies stand a few metres apart on either side of a fence.

Getting here is not like arriving at most passes. Access is controlled, and a permit is required that has to be arranged in Gangtok. The pass is open only on certain days, and regulations about who can go change, so check locally. Foreign nationals have often been barred from this stretch, and visitors are in practice accompanied by registered vehicles. The road itself, from Gangtok, climbs in a long series of hairpins through forest and then bare alpine ground, and it is a serious mountain road: narrow, sometimes broken by landslides in monsoon, and often wrapped in cloud.

The altitude makes its own demands. At more than four thousand metres, you can feel your pulse and your breath, and if you are not acclimatised a quick dash from Gangtok can bring headaches or nausea. Move slowly, drink water, and do not stay long if you feel unwell. The weather can switch from bright sun to freezing fog in minutes, and snow can fall in any month except high summer. In winter the road can be shut entirely.

On the way up you pass Tsomgo Lake, a glacial lake that freezes in winter and draws crowds in season, and the Baba Mandir, a shrine to a soldier remembered as a protector of the road. These are the practical rest points, with tea stalls, hot snacks and a few souvenir shops, and the army maintains a presence along the whole route.

Gangtok, about twenty-three kilometres away, is the only sensible place to fill up, and you should do it before leaving. Carry warm clothes, gloves and something to eat. The silence at the top, apart from the wind and the flags, is quite memorable, and the view across to the Tibetan plateau is the thing you will remember.
t.aritar@27.2,88.7:
Aritar is a small village in the east of Sikkim, close to the border with West Bengal, and its great attraction is a lake. Aritar Lake, also called Lampokhari, lies in a fold of the hills with green slopes around it, and locals take boats out on the water at weekends. The village lies on an old branch of the Silk Route that once carried wool, salt and tea between Tibet and the plains of India through the Nathu La pass. The nearest towns are Rangpo, about fifteen kilometres away, and the capital Gangtok, about seventeen, and the bigger one has the fuel stations and shops.

The riding in this part of Sikkim is typically Himalayan foothills: narrow roads clinging to steep slopes, hairpins following hairpins, deep valleys filled with cloud, and terraced fields where farmers grow rice, maize and cardamom. The surface can vary from smooth tarmac to potholes and landslide damage, especially after the monsoon, which arrives in June and lasts until September. Land slips are common, and trucks and shared jeeps use the same roads, so keep to your side and sound the horn on blind corners, as local drivers do.

The Silk Route circuit is rich in history. Sikkim was an independent Buddhist kingdom ruled by the Chogyal until it joined India in 1975, and the old trade link to Lhasa shaped its culture. Monasteries in the hills fly prayer flags, and in the valleys you see white flags planted for the dead. People here are a mix of Lepcha, Bhutia and Nepali communities, and the food reflects that: steamed momos, thukpa noodle soup, and strong milky tea.

For a rider, the best seasons are October to December and March to May, when skies are clear and the mountains show. On a good morning, you may see Kanchenjunga, the third highest peak in the world, shimmering white far to the north. Plan fuel carefully, because small villages like Aritar do not count on a pump, and carry some cash, as cards are unreliable. A homestay by the lake with dal bhat and a view across the water is a fine way to end the day.
t.talnakh@69.5,88.4:
Talnakh lies well above the Arctic Circle, a city of about fifty-nine thousand people built at the foot of the Kharaelakh Mountains on the Taimyr Peninsula, and it exists because of what is underneath it. The ground here holds some of the richest nickel and copper deposits in the world, and the mines and smelters of Norilsk, sixteen kilometres to the southwest, dominate the economy. The city grew from the 1960s onwards as a company town, with blocks of flats raised on piles because the permafrost would otherwise melt and swallow them.

It is an extraordinary place to visit, and an unusual one to include on a ride. Norilsk and Talnakh are not connected to the main Russian road network, so reaching them means flying in or arriving by ship on the Yenisei in summer, and a motorcycle must come the same way. Foreign visitors also need special permission, since Norilsk has long been a restricted area, so check the rules well in advance. Once there, the local roads are short and mostly asphalt, with fuel stations, shops and cafes in both cities, and you can ride in the tundra around the town.

The climate is fierce. Winter lasts around eight months, with temperatures of minus thirty or lower and a polar night that lasts for weeks around the solstice, when the sun does not rise above the horizon. In summer the opposite happens, with a midnight sun that shines through the night and a short, intense burst of green. Snow can fall in any month, and the best time for a visit is July and August, when the tundra flowers and the light is long and low.

The air carries a story as well. The smelters have long released sulphur dioxide, which has damaged the vegetation for many kilometres around, and the legacy of industry here is visible and sobering. Beyond it lies the Putorana Plateau, a vast area of flat-topped mountains, deep lakes and waterfalls recognised as a World Heritage Site, which is reached by boat or helicopter rather than by road. Talnakh gives you a view of humans working at the edge of what is possible, and it deserves respect and a warm coat.
t.upper tsagaan gol@49.1,88.3:
Far out in Mongolia's westernmost corner, where the country wedges itself between Russia, China and Kazakhstan, the Altai mountains rise to the glaciated crown of Tavan Bogd. Below them the Tsagaan Gol, the White River, runs through valleys of larch and bare rock, and on the walls above the water prehistoric hunters carved some of the finest petroglyphs in Central Asia. They are part of the Petroglyphic Complexes of the Mongolian Altai, a UNESCO listing that spans thousands of years, from around the end of the Ice Age through the Bronze Age to the early Turkic era. The images show ibex, aurochs, deer, camels, hunters with bows, and in the later layers horsemen and chariots.

The effect of the carvings is not in any single image but in the density of them, and in the knowledge that people looked at this same river long before anyone wrote a word. Some panels are weathered nearly flat, others have a crisp edge when the sun rakes across. The valley is also the homeland of the Kazakh and Tuvan herders of Bayan-Ölgii, with their felt gers, long-legged horses, and in winter the eagle hunters who ride out with golden eagles on the arm.

Riding to it is serious expedition travel. There is very little paved road in this part of Mongolia, and the way in from Ölgii, the provincial capital, follows tracks across steppe, gravel flats and river fords that change from one year to the next. A capable adventure bike, a companion, a satellite messenger and good tyre-repair kit are ordinary parts of the plan, and many riders choose to go with a local guide or a support vehicle. The season is short, mostly from June to September, with snow possible at any time at altitude, and rivers swollen in July.

No settlement is listed nearby on the data, which tells you something. Ölgii has fuel, shops and guesthouses, and you should stock up on petrol, food and drinking water there, because beyond it supplies are patchy. Nights are cold even in summer, and weather can turn from sun to sleet within an hour. Camping is common and generally welcomed, but ask before pitching on pasture, and take your rubbish out. Border zones in the Altai require a permit, so check this before you set out.
t.petroglyphic complexes of the mongolian:
The Mongolian Altai does not look like the landscape of a rock-art gallery. It looks like open ground, grey and gold in the light, with snow mountains standing far off along the border of China and Russia. And yet near here, in the far west of Bayan-Ulgii province, the rocks hold thousands of petroglyphs, some of them thought to be many thousands of years old. Tsagaan Salaa and Baga Oigor are the best known. Aral Tolgoi is a neighbouring part of the same inscribed group.

The pictures are pecked into dark stone: hunters with bows, ibex, mammoth-like beasts in the oldest layers, later horses and chariots, and Turkic-era riders. They span the end of the Ice Age through the Bronze Age to the medieval period. No one is sure why people kept returning to carve here, but the valley clearly mattered, and the sense of continuity is hard to shake. Standing in front of an animal drawn long before anyone wrote anything down is a quiet thing.

The people of this province are mostly Kazakhs, and the region is known for its eagle hunters. In winter, hunters on horseback go out with golden eagles, and families live in felt gers in the summer pastures. You may meet shepherds who are curious about a motorcycle, and if invited for tea or salty milk tea, accept.

The riding is expedition-level. Tracks are rough and often just parallel scars across the steppe, rivers have to be crossed, and weather in the Altai can turn from sun to snow in one afternoon even in summer. Fuel and supplies are in Olgii, the provincial capital, which is a long way from here, so carry spare fuel and enough water, and tell someone your route. Best time is June to September. Come with a bike you trust and a day to spare, because the place rewards a slow pace and bad ground punishes a fast one.
t.aral tolgoi@48.7,88.1:
Aral Tolgoi sits on a bend of open ground in the Altai of western Mongolia, in the province of Bayan-Ulgii, where the land climbs steadily toward the borders with China and Russia. The name has the sound of a place: tolgoi means a hill or head, and aral an island, so think of a rise standing out in flat, braided ground, perhaps once surrounded by channels of the river nearby. It is part of the same ancient story as the petroglyph sites that lie along these valleys.

What is inscribed in the rock here is a record of people who passed through for thousands of years: hunters, herders, horsemen, warriors. The pictures are simple, pecked animals and humans, repeated and layered. For anyone who likes archaeology, there is a pleasure in finding them yourself, without a visitor centre or a rope. That also means it is your job to leave them as you found them, so do not touch the surface and do not park on anything that looks like old stone.

Around you the landscape is huge and nearly empty. Snow peaks shimmer to the west, the valleys are pale with dry grass, and you might see a herd of goats moving slowly up a slope, or a lone rider heading somewhere you cannot imagine. Kazakh families, who make up most of this province, live in felt tents in summer and in low houses in winter, and eagle hunters train golden eagles for the winter hunt.

The ride is gravel and dirt, with water crossings and sandy stretches, and it is not a place for a first adventure. Fuel is available in the provincial centre, Olgii, and in Khovd to the east, and not at the site. Carry extra. Mobile signal is patchy. Summer, from June to September, is the time to go, and a day with clear skies gives the best light for rock carvings and the best views of the mountains.
t.tsomgo lake@27.4,88.8:
Tsomgo Lake, also called Changu, sits at about 3,750 metres in the mountains east of Gangtok, a small oval of cold water cupped in a bowl of bare slopes. It is a glacial lake, fed by melting snow, and it freezes over in winter, when the surrounding hills are white. The Sikkimese hold it sacred, and local lamas once used the colour of its water to foretell the year ahead. In spring the banks are bright with primulas and rhododendrons, and in autumn the air is sharp and clear.

The road to the lake is part of the old trade route that once carried wool, tea and salt between Sikkim and Tibet, and it continues up to the Nathu La pass on the Chinese border at more than four thousand metres. Because this is a border area, visitors need a permit, which has to be arranged in Gangtok through a registered agent or the tourist office, and the army controls access to the higher parts of the road. Rules change from time to time, so check them before you set off.

The ride up from Gangtok is steep and spectacular, with a long run of hairpin bends through forests of rhododendron and fir, then out into open, high pasture. The surface is often rough, with landslides, potholes and patches of ice, and fog can arrive without notice, cutting visibility to a few metres. Winter snow can close the road for days at a time, and the best months are from April to June and from September to November. At this altitude, many people feel the effects of thin air, with headaches and shortness of breath, so go slowly and drink water.

Gangtok, about sixteen kilometres away as the crow flies but much further by road, is the nearest town with proper fuel and supplies, so fill up there and carry an extra layer, since it can be freezing even on a sunny day. The sunlight at this height is strong, so bring sunglasses and sun cream.
t.zuluk@27.3,88.8:
Zuluk is a village strung along a ridge in the eastern Himalayas, on the old Silk Route that once connected Sikkim with Tibet, and it is a very different place from the busy tourist spots of Gangtok. The village is small, with a few homestays, an army post and a prayer-flag-covered hillside, at around three thousand metres. On clear mornings, the sunrise lights up the peaks of Kanchenjunga, the third highest mountain in the world, which seems to float above the clouds.

The road is the main attraction. Just above the village, the track from Zuluk to Thambi viewpoint climbs the mountainside in a series of tight, stacked hairpins, thirty-odd bends in all, and from the top the road looks like a ribbon of thread dropped on the slope. The road was part of the old trade route and was used by traders carrying wool, yak butter and tea, and later by British expeditions to Tibet. Today, the route is mainly used by the army and by visitors, so the traffic is light, but the surface is often rough, with loose gravel, potholes and landslides, especially after rain.

The ride from Gangtok to Zuluk is long and demanding, taking most of a day. The road winds through forests of oak and rhododendron, past villages and tea plantations, then climbs into high, open country, with big views and almost no traffic. The weather can change quickly, with fog and drizzle common, and in winter snow and ice make the road dangerous. The best time for riding is from March to May and from October to November, when the skies are clearest.

Because Zuluk is in a border area, a permit is required, and it must be arranged in advance through an agent in Gangtok. Fuel is not available in the village, so fill up in Gangtok or Rangpo, and carry spare if you can, since distances are long and stations are few. Homestays offer simple rooms and hot meals, with rice, dal, vegetables and sometimes yak cheese, and electricity can be unreliable, so bring a torch and warm clothes for the cold nights.
t.gangtok@27.3,88.6:
Gangtok sits on a ridge in the Himalayan foothills of Sikkim, at about 1,650 metres, and on a clear morning you can see Kangchenjunga, the third-highest mountain in the world at 8,586 metres, floating pink above the clouds. Sikkim was an independent Buddhist kingdom until it joined India in 1975, and the culture is still a mix of Lepcha, Bhutia and Nepali traditions, with prayer flags on the rooftops, monasteries on the hills and a feeling of calm that surprises people coming from the plains. The state became the first in India to be fully organic in its farming, and the cities are noticeably clean.

The centre is MG Marg, a pedestrian street with cafés, shops and benches where families walk in the evening, and everything is built on steep slopes, with stairs and winding lanes linking the layers. Rumtek monastery, a few kilometres outside the city, is a major seat of Tibetan Buddhism, with golden roofs and the chanting of monks. Momos, thukpa noodle soup and fermented vegetables are the local food, and a hot cup of butter tea does not appeal to everyone, but it is a classic.

The Silk Route in the name of the ride refers to the old trade path to Tibet over the Nathu La pass at about 4,300 metres, which was an important link for wool, salt and tea until the border closed in 1962. It reopened for limited trade in 2006. Foreign visitors and many others need a special permit to travel on that road and to Tsomgo Lake, which lies at nearly 3,800 metres, so arrange it through an agent in advance. The roads climb in tight switchbacks through rhododendron forest and then bare rocky ground, with sudden fog, landslides in the monsoon and bitterly cold air at the top.

Gangtok is a city of thirty thousand with fuel stations on its main roads, but down in the Teesta valley, Singtam is a fifteen-kilometre run away and offers more choice. Fill the tank before climbing, as the roads are long and services few. The best time to ride is from March to May and from October to November, when the skies are clear and the rhododendrons bloom, and monsoon rains from June to September can close roads.
t.tsagaan salaa baga oigor@49.3,88.4:
The far west of Mongolia belongs to a different world from the grasslands near Ulaanbaatar. Bayan-Ölgii province lies in the Altai Mountains, close to the borders of Russia, China and Kazakhstan, and most of its people are ethnic Kazakhs who arrived in the nineteenth century and still keep eagles for hunting. In winter, riders on horseback go out with golden eagles on their arms to hunt foxes, a tradition that survives here more strongly than anywhere else. The air is dry and thin, and the sky seems enormous.

The sites of Tsagaan Salaa and Baga Oigor are part of the Petroglyphic Complexes of the Mongolian Altai, which UNESCO inscribed in 2011. They lie along the valley of the Tsagaan Salaa River, where thousands of images have been pecked into the dark rock. The earliest are some twelve thousand years old, depicting hunters and animals such as ibex, deer and aurochs, and later layers add chariots, bronze age burial mounds and Turkic stone figures from the first millennium. Walking among them, with the wind in the grass and a few yaks nearby, you can read the long human story of the mountains.

For riders this is true expedition terrain. The tracks that lead into the valleys are rough and unmarked, crossing rivers and open steppe, with loose gravel and soft sand, and the weather can change in an hour. Snow can fall at any time of year at this altitude, and the best months are July and August, when the days are warm and the nights cold. There are no signs and navigation relies on a GPS and local knowledge. A guide who knows the tracks and the river crossings is not a luxury here but a safety measure.

Ölgii, the provincial capital, is the last place with proper fuel stations, shops and a bazaar, and it makes sense to fill tanks and carry spare fuel before going into the mountains. Nomad families welcome travelers into their gers with salty milk tea, dried curds and sometimes boiled mutton, and a polite visitor accepts what is offered.

The land is huge and the stillness is real. At dusk the light goes gold on the hills, and the only sounds are the river and the occasional call of a herder.
t.ukok quiet zone on the ukok plateau@49.4:
The Ukok Plateau is where Russia runs out of room. At around two thousand meters, in the far south of the Altai Republic, a wide cold steppe lies pinned between the borders of Kazakhstan, China and Mongolia, with snow peaks on the horizon and permafrost under the grass. It is part of the Golden Mountains of Altai, a UNESCO site listed in 1998, and the Russian authorities named it a Quiet Zone to protect the landscape and the traditions of the people who live and herd animals here.

Its fame comes from the grave. In 1993 archaeologists digging in a burial mound on the plateau found a woman, about twenty-five years old, preserved in ice, with elaborate tattoos on her arms and a tall felt headdress. She belonged to the Pazyryk culture, horse-riding nomads who lived here about two and a half thousand years ago. Journalists called her the Ice Maiden, and the Altai people call her the Princess of Ukok and consider the removal of her body a profanation. Some local people connect the earthquakes that struck the region in the following years with her absence, which tells you how alive the story still is.

For a rider, the plateau is an expedition goal rather than a day out. The approach is the Chuya Highway, a long and beautiful road from Gorno-Altaysk through the mountains to Kosh-Agach and the Mongolian border, with grand views of rivers the color of milky turquoise. Beyond the last settlements the tracks become rough, braided across streams and bogs. Because the plateau lies in the border zone, permits are required, and entering without them is not an option. A local operator is essential.

The weather is harsh and unpredictable. Snow can fall in any month, and the summer window is short, with the best conditions from July to early September. Wind scours the open ground, and nights are cold even in midsummer.

Fuel is the main limit. Kosh-Agach is the last real stop, a windswept town with stations and a few shops, and nothing waits beyond it. Carry spare fuel, food and a proper repair kit. The silence on the plateau is deep, broken only by the wind and the occasional cry of a bird of prey.
t.tashanta@49.7,89.2:
The road ends here, almost literally. Tashanta is the Russian border post on the Chuysky Trakt, a tiny settlement high in the dry southeast corner of the Altai Republic at about two thousand metres, where the highway that began far back in Biysk reaches the Mongolian frontier. There is not much more to it than customs buildings, a few houses and a very big sky. Kosh-Agach, the nearest town of any size, lies a long drive back to the northwest, so fuel and supplies belong to that town, not here.

The ride up is among the most dramatic in southern Siberia. After Kosh-Agach the road crosses the Chuya steppe, a high, dry basin ringed with snow peaks, where the vegetation turns to short grass and the wind never stops. The tarmac is fairly straight, with long, open stretches, and the real challenge is the weather: crosswinds, sudden cold, and in winter extreme frost. Summer is the sensible season, and even then you should pack warm gear. The light is fierce and clear, with distances that deceive, and the peaks of the Southern Chuya range stand white above the steppe.

The border here is a controlled area, and visiting requires the right documents and permission, which change over time, so check current rules before you set out. Treat the border post with respect and avoid photographing military or customs installations. The crossing into Mongolia lies beyond, in a region of high plateaus and nomadic herders, where Kazakh and Mongolian cultures meet. Until the twentieth century this was the old caravan route for tea, silk and furs, and the Chuya steppe has seen travellers for thousands of years.

Nature is stark and beautiful. The steppe is home to marmots, hawks, falcons and steppe eagles, and in the nearby mountains live argali sheep and snow leopards, though a rider is very unlikely to meet any of them. Salt lakes and streams dot the basin, and the soil is stony and pale. At night, the sky is crowded with stars, and the cold is sharp.

Bring more fuel than you think you need, plus water, food and warm layers, and tell someone your plan. Mobile coverage is poor, and help is far away. The reward is the feeling of having reached an actual edge.

Norilsk is the northernmost city of its size on Earth, sitting well above the Arctic Circle on the Taimyr Peninsula, and it is not connected by road to the rest of Russia. Everything arrives by air, by river and sea through Dudinka, or by the railway that runs down to the port. The city, around 140,000 people, and its neighbour Talnakh, about 59,000, exist for one reason: a spectacularly rich deposit of nickel, copper and palladium found beneath the tundra.

That makes any ride here a local one, a short run on the roads within the mining and industrial district, with Talnakh the most obvious destination. Fuel and food are in the city, and the roads in town are straight, broad and surfaced, though frost heaves can be rough. Wind howls across open ground, and snow can arrive in any month of the year. The summer season, a few weeks around July, brings a midnight sun, with light all through the night, and then the long polar night follows in winter, when darkness lasts for weeks and temperatures fall far below freezing. Foreign visitors need special permission to enter the area, so check rules in advance.

The history of Norilsk is dark. The city was founded in the 1930s as a forced-labour camp complex, and thousands of prisoners built the first mines, smelters and housing. The camp system closed in the 1950s, but the industry stayed, and today the city is among the most polluted in the world, with smelter smoke streaking the horizon. It is, strangely, also a place with a proud, close-knit community, and the Soviet-era architecture in the centre has a strict, handsome geometry, with buildings arranged to shelter streets from the wind.

The nature around is bleak and magnificent. The Putorana Plateau, a vast flat-topped mountain range with deep lakes and countless waterfalls, lies to the east and is a UNESCO World Heritage site, reachable mainly by helicopter or boat. The tundra blooms briefly in July, with dwarf birch, cloudberries and reindeer moss, and reindeer herds move across the land. Arctic foxes, snowy owls and wild reindeer are the wildlife.

Do not treat this as a casual stop. Dress for extreme cold even in summer, drink hot drinks, watch for ice on the roads and keep a close eye on weather alerts.
